nameStory: The 'crisped pincushion' gets its name from two distinctive features that make it easy to remember. When dry, its leaves curl and crisp up dramatically, giving it a wrinkled appearance, while its overall growth form creates tight, rounded cushions that look just like little pincushions stuck to tree bark.
description: Crisped pincushion moss is a small but eye-catching moss that forms dense, rounded cushions on tree bark throughout New England. These compact mounds rarely grow larger than a few inches across, creating what looks like dozens of tiny green pincushions dotting the trunks of trees. The moss is acrocarpous, meaning it grows upright rather than creeping, with sporophytes (spore-bearing structures) that emerge from the tips of the stems. Its most distinctive feature is how dramatically it changes appearance between wet and dry conditions.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tight, dome-shaped cushions that feel firm and springy when pressed, typically 1-3 inches across and growing directly on tree bark

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: When wet, leaves are straight and green; when dry, they curl and twist dramatically, creating a distinctly crinkled, crisped texture that feels rough to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when moist, turning yellowish-green to brown when dry, with the color change being quite dramatic and noticeable

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Small capsules on short stalks emerge from cushion centers, often with a distinctive ribbed or grooved appearance when mature

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on tree bark, particularly favoring the trunk and larger branches rather than twigs or rocks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Cushions feel dense and compact, almost like a firm sponge when wet, but become stiff and brittle-feeling when completely dry

habitat: Look for crisped pincushion moss on the bark of deciduous and coniferous trees throughout New England's forests, from sea level to moderate elevations. It particularly favors trees in somewhat open areas where it receives good light but isn't constantly wet, such as forest edges, parklands, and mature woodlands. You'll rarely find it on rocks or soil—it's almost exclusively a tree-dwelling moss.

seasonality.spring: Cushions begin to green up and become more prominent as moisture returns. Sporophytes may be developing, appearing as small bumps in the center of cushions.
seasonality.summer: Most active growing season when cushions are fullest and greenest during wet periods, though they may appear quite brown and crispy during dry spells.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes mature and release spores, while cushions remain visible and may show their characteristic crisping more frequently as humidity drops.
seasonality.winter: Cushions persist and remain identifiable, often appearing more brownish but still maintaining their distinctive shape and bark-dwelling habit.

funFact: Crisped pincushion moss can lose up to 95% of its water content and appear completely dead, then fully revive and turn bright green again within minutes of getting wet—a superpower that allows it to survive in the relatively harsh environment of tree bark where water comes and goes quickly.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small cushion mosses on trees, but the dramatic leaf curling when dry is your best clue—if you see a brownish, extremely crinkled cushion on bark that looks almost dead, it's probably crisped pincushion waiting for water. Memory trick: 'Crisped and crispy when dry!'
compareHints: Compared to its relatives in the Ulota genus, crisped pincushion shows the most dramatic leaf curling when dry—much more pronounced than Hutchins' pincushion or club pincushion. While all Ulota species form cushions on bark, crisped pincushion's leaves become so tightly curled and twisted when dry that the cushions can look almost dead, whereas its relatives maintain a more normal appearance even when moisture is low.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Crisped Pincushion (Ulota crispa), Curly Ulota has more uniformly curled leaves and tends to form denser cushions.

Hutchins' Pincushion forms the tightest, most perfectly dome-shaped cushions of all the Ulota species in New England, while Crisped Pincushion spreads more loosely and Club Pincushion tends to grow in more elongated patches.
Among the pincushion mosses, Club Pincushion is distinguished by its very short sporophyte stalks compared to Crisped Pincushion's longer ones.
Compared to the more common crisped pincushion (Ulota crispa), Ulota intermedia forms smaller, more compact cushions and typically has shorter, less prominently curled leaves when dry.
